text: PSR J0952−0607 is a massive millisecond pulsar in a binary system located between 3,200–5,700 light-years (970–1,740 pc) from Earth in the constellation Sextans, with its distance highly uncertain.[2][3][4] As of 2022[update], it holds the record for being the most massive neutron star known, with a mass of 2.35±0.17 times that of the Sun—potentially near the Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff mass upper limit for neutron stars.[4][7] The pulsar rotates at a frequency of 707.31 Hz (a period of 1.4137 ms), making it the second-fastest-spinning pulsar known and the fastest-spinning pulsar in the Milky Way.[8][6] It was discovered by the Low-Frequency Array (LOFAR) radio telescope during a 2016 search for pulsars.[6] Classified as a black widow pulsar, it has a closely-orbiting substellar-mass companion (less than 0.1 M☉)[9]: 127  that is being ablated by the pulsar's intense high-energy solar winds and gamma-ray emissions.[4][9] The system's high-energy emissions have been detected in gamma-ray and X-ray wavelengths.[10][3][11] PSR J0952−0607 was first identified as an unassociated gamma-ray source during the first seven years of the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope's all-sky survey since 2008.[8]: 2  Due to its location away from the Galactic Center and its pulsar-like gamma-ray emission peak at 1.4 GeV, it was considered a prime millisecond pulsar candidate.[8]: 2  The pulsar was confirmed by LOFAR on 25 December 2016, revealing a 707-Hz radio pulsation frequency and radial acceleration from an unseen binary companion.[8]: 3  Follow-up observations occurred from January to February 2017 with LOFAR and in March 2017 with the Green Bank Telescope; optical observations by the 2.54-meter Isaac Newton Telescope on La Palma in January 2017 detected and confirmed the companion at an apparent magnitude of 23.[8]: 3  The discovery was published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters and announced in a NASA press release in September 2017.[8][6] The binary system consists of the massive pulsar and a substellar-mass companion orbiting at a distance of 1.6 million km (1 million mi)[a] with an orbital period of 6.42 hours.[4] The companion is likely tidally locked, with one hemisphere always facing the pulsar, and its orbit is oriented nearly face-on with an inclination of 60°, as indicated by the absence of eclipses and lack of modulation in pulsar signals, suggesting a circular orbit with negligible eccentricity.[4]: 4  The companion, likely a former star reduced to the size of a large gas giant or brown dwarf, has a present-day mass of 0.032±0.002 M☉ or 34±2 MJ,[4]: 4  and is bloated to up to 80% of its Roche lobe due to intense irradiation, glowing with a thermal luminosity of about 10 L☉,[b] contributing significantly to the system's optical brightness.[4]: 1, 4 [2]: 1  Its low density, likely around 10 g/cm³ (with significant uncertainty due to the unknown distance), makes it susceptible to tidal deformation.[2]: 11  The irradiated hemisphere reaches a temperature of 6,200 K, while the unirradiated hemisphere remains at 3,000 K, resulting in a hemispherical luminosity difference and brightness variability greater than one magnitude, as seen in the optical light curve.[2]: 4 [3]: 8  The pulsar likely gained most of its mass by accreting up to 1 M☉ of material from its companion.[4]: 5  With a standard neutron star radius of 10 km (6.2 mi), the equator rotates at over 44,400 km/s (27,600 mi/s)—about 14% the speed of light.[13] Based on 7 years of precise pulsation data, the rotation period is slowing at a rate less than 4.6×10⁻²¹ seconds per second, corresponding to a characteristic age of 4.9 billion years.[3]: 11  The pulsar has a remarkably weak surface magnetic field of 6.1×10⁷ gauss (6.1×10³ T), placing it among the 10 weakest known pulsar magnetic fields as of 2022[update], compared to typical pulsar fields of around 1×10¹² G (1.0×10⁸ T), over 10,000 times stronger.[14][4]: 1  Possible explanations for this weakness include accreted matter burying the surface field or heat-driven evolution of the solid crust.[14]: 1–2 [4]: 1  PSR J0952−0607 appears very faint in gamma-rays and was not detected in July 2011.[11][3]: 2
